citeAs: Talmor, Alon, Jonathan Herzig, Nicholas Lourie, and Jonathan Berant. (2019). CommonsenseQA: A Question Answering Challenge Targeting Commonsense Knowledge. arXiv.
creator: Alon Talmor, Jonathan Herzig, Nicholas Lourie, Jonathan Berant (Tel-Aviv University; Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence)
description: CommonsenseQA is a multiple-choice question answering dataset for commonsense reasoning built from ConceptNet. Crowd workers author questions that mention a source concept and distinguish among semantically related target concepts, yielding 12,247 questions with five answer choices each.
name: CommonsenseQA
publisher: Tel-Aviv University; Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence
rai:annotatorDemographics: Questions were generated and verified by Amazon Mechanical Turk workers. 122 formulators contributed to question generation, though 10 workers formulated more than 85% of the questions.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Each question was verified by 2 workers, and only questions verified by at least one worker who answered correctly were kept. This verification process filtered out 15% of the questions.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: For each ConceptNet question set, AMT workers saw one question concept and three answer concepts and were asked to formulate three questions, each containing the question concept and having one designated answer concept as correct but not the other two. Workers then added two distractors per question, and a disjoint group of workers verified whether the question was answerable or selected the correct answer.
rai:dataBiases: The paper explicitly notes that web text omits much commonsense information due to reporting bias, motivating freely authored questions that require background knowledge. It also discusses avoiding simple surface clues and random distractors by grouping semantically similar target concepts and instructing workers not to use words strongly related to the answer concept.
rai:dataCollection: The dataset was created by extracting filtered triplets and question sets from ConceptNet, then using Amazon Mechanical Turk workers to author three questions per subgraph, add two additional distractors per question, verify question quality, and finally retrieve Google search snippets as optional context.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The source data were ConceptNet triplets. The authors filtered ConceptNet's 32 million triplets and used subgraphs with one source concept and three target concepts sharing the same relation as the basis for question generation.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping
rai:dataLimitations: The paper shows that current models perform far below humans on the benchmark and notes that retrieved web snippets do not appear to carry much useful information. It also highlights remaining difficulty from examples involving negation, antonyms, factoid knowledge, finer-grained distinctions, and conjunctions of conditions.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The authors filtered ConceptNet edges with rule-based constraints, grouped triplets into question sets with one source concept and three semantically related target concepts, added one distractor from ConceptNet and one manually authored distractor to each question, filtered out 15% of questions through human verification, and retrieved 100 Google result snippets for each of the five answer candidates as optional context.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Before crowdsourcing, the authors filtered ConceptNet triplets by removing general relations such as RelatedTo and well-explored relations such as IsA, excluding concepts longer than four words or not in English, and filtering triplets whose two concepts had very low edit distance.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for evaluating and advancing question answering and natural language understanding systems on commonsense reasoning, and for studying what current models capture or miss about commonsense knowledge.
